A Group's posts are the Create/Announce activities in its outbox, and its members are its followers. The bare Lemmy fields are the instance's own, but they are not iris:-namespaced, so they survive that stamping. An Iris community never emits the bare Lemmy fields (it renders its equivalents under the iris: namespace), so it is not misclassified.

member.name: T:Iris.Client.Pipeline.ProxyFallbackHandler
member.summary: A that implements Phase 6's proxy fallback: when a request to a remote ActivityPub instance is rejected with 401/403 (the remote instance cannot validate the client's signature — the browser has no signed outbound, or the actor's key is not resolvable cross-origin), the handler retries the request through the home instance's proxy endpoint (POST {proxyBase}/ap/v1/proxy/{target}) with Basic auth. The proxy identifies the actor from the credentials and signs the forwarded request with the actor's key, which the remote instance can validate.
member.remarks:
The handler is the outermost stage of the client pipeline (it wraps the whole → → chain). The direct attempt is fully signed (the runs inside); when it is rejected 401/403 the handler strips the direct-attempt Signature (the proxy will re-sign) and forwards the request to the proxy as a POST with a Basic-auth Authorization header. The proxy relays the remote response, which the handler returns.
Only 401/403 on the direct attempt trigger a fallback; a successful direct response is returned unchanged. A proxy failure (the proxy itself returns 401/403/5xx) is returned as-is — the handler does not loop.
Cross-instance reads (Phase 22.4 / US-8): a browser cannot reach a cross-origin remote instance directly — a direct cross-origin GET is blocked by CORS, which surfaces as a network failure with no status code, so the 401/403 fallback never engages and the read fails. In this mode (the crossInstanceReadsViaProxy constructor argument) a GET whose host differs from the dial base (the instance the browser can reach directly) is routed straight through the same-origin home proxy before any direct attempt — the proxy relays it to the remote instance and returns the response, so the browser only ever talks to its own origin. A same-host GET (a read of the local instance) dials directly, as before.
Cookie-auth mode: when credentials is the proxy request carries no Authorization header. Because the proxy request is same-origin, the browser's transport attaches the site cookie, and the proxy identifies the acting actor from the cookie's actor_iri claim (the same cookie-auth fallback the local mute / media endpoints use). This is how the Blazor WebAssembly client routes cross-instance reads: the browser has no Basic credentials, so it authenticates to its own instance by cookie.
